title: What AI actually is
paras: Let me start with what AI actually is, because everything follows from it. When we say AI we nearly always mean large language models — the chat assistants that draft, summarise and answer questions. Each is a prediction engine: trained on a huge quantity of text, it generates the most statistically plausible next words. It holds no verified database of planning law, and it doesn't check whether what it produces is true — it just produces text that reads as if it were.

That one property explains both halves. It's why they're useful — fluent drafting, quick summarising — and why they're dangerous: the model states something false with the same confidence as something correct, because it optimises for plausibility, not accuracy. So treat an output as a draft to be checked; treat it as an authority and you'll be embarrassed. The precise references and dates all live in the written guide — I'll stay on the ideas.

title: What it genuinely helps with today
paras: So what helps today? The strongest use, in use now, is drafting — reports, letters, representations, consultation responses — and re-drafting for tone, length or plain English. The model gets words on the page; you supply the facts and the judgement. Nearly as mature is summarising long documents and background research — condensing a big evidence base, or orienting fast on an unfamiliar topic. The catch: a summary can quietly drop the one qualification that mattered, so check it against the source rather than treat it as a substitute for reading it.

The most dangerous use, and barely reliable yet, is searching case law and appeal decisions. General models are notorious for inventing citations — an appeal reference that doesn't exist, or a case name pinned to the wrong facts. Lawyers have been sanctioned for filing fabricated citations, and planners face the same trap. So treat any legal or appeal reference from a general model as unverified until you've found it in the primary source. Tools grounded in a real, named database are better — but know which kind you're using.

Several other uses are genuine but emerging. Stress-testing your own reasoning — argue the other side, find the gap in your case — is sound, because you stay the judge. Preliminary site and constraints work is only as good as the data the tool can see: a general chat model has no live constraint data, so it guesses; the useful versions plug into real datasets. Validation and completeness checking is advancing fast. Appeal analysis and pattern-spotting is promising but unreliable on specifics. Design tools produce impressions and moodboards, not accurate survey-based visualisations — never pass them off as such. The thread: the closer a use sits to a verifiable fact, the harder you check.

title: The risks — the heart of the matter
paras: Now the risks — the heart of it. First, hallucination: the confident falsehood. Because it generates plausible text, the model will produce a fabricated appeal decision, a mis-stated policy, or a national-policy paragraph that doesn't exist — indistinguishable from a correct answer. In planning that's serious: an appeal that can't be found, a condition test quoted wrongly, a heritage duty inverted. So verify every factual output against the primary source before it leaves your desk — every case, every policy reference, every figure. If you can't verify it, you can't use it.

Second, professional responsibility. The judgement, advice and decision stay yours. An output is evidence to check, never an answer to adopt — your name on a document means you own every word, whatever produced the draft. It engages the professional Code and its duties of competence, integrity and honesty: competence means understanding the tool enough to catch its errors; integrity means never presenting unverified output as your professional opinion. And it's for you to decide how, if and when to use it.

Third, confidentiality and data protection. Paste text into a third-party tool and you send someone else's information to someone else's computer — and many public tools may retain your inputs to train future models. Client details, personal data on objectors or applicants, commercially sensitive scheme information — none of it belongs there without thought. Under data protection law you're the controller: you need a lawful basis, transparency and security. So keep sensitive material out of public tools; on live matters use an enterprise product whose terms exclude your inputs from training and give a data-processing agreement; anonymise first; and read the terms.

Fourth, bias, currency and over-reliance. A model reflects its training data, gaps and slants included, and has a knowledge cut-off — so unless it's given them, it may misstate the current Framework or a recent Act. And over-reliance erodes skill: a planner who stops reading the source because the summary's quicker loses the ability to notice when it's wrong. The tool should sharpen judgement, not replace the habits that formed it.

And fifth, transparency and disclosure — now a procedural duty. The Planning Inspectorate's guidance says parties may use AI to prepare submissions, but that it's your responsibility to ensure what's generated is accurate and appropriate, and that professional parties must comply with their codes. Where AI produced evidence, disclose it — that it was used, which tool, for what, and what you checked. It warns AI can create fake evidence, and says plainly: use it responsibly. If a decision is challenged, showing what you produced, checked and disclosed is your protection.

title: How to use AI well
paras: So how do you use it well? A handful of rules, the same whether you're solo or a large consultancy. Use AI for drafting and research, never for final facts. Verify every citation and policy reference against the primary source. Keep confidential and personal material out of public tools. Treat every output as a starting point, not a product. Know the question well enough to spot a wrong answer. And keep a record of your own reasoning, so the judgement is demonstrably yours.

Behind those sits one truth: AI rewards the expert and traps the novice. Because the output is always fluent, it's most dangerous to the person least able to catch its errors. An experienced planner reads a draft and sees the three things it got wrong — the misremembered policy, the optimistic assumption, the missing constraint. A junior sees a finished answer. The tool doesn't lower the expertise the job needs; it raises it — catching a confident error takes more knowledge than writing from scratch.

title: Where it is heading
paras: So where's it heading? Better grounding — tying the model to real, named data, so it has less room to invent. Planning-specific assistants that answer against a named Local Plan, rather than the whole internet, are the most promising step, because a model made to cite an actual policy hallucinates far less. Automated pre-submission validation is emerging too, backed by Government pilots. Reasoning over connected planning data — knowledge graphs that grasp how designations, policies and constraints relate, rather than matching keywords — is on the horizon. And AI-assisted design and assessment advances as the data improves.

Government activity shows the trajectory. The department's Extract tool is now live to all English planning authorities, turning historic documents into structured data. And a decision-support prototype — built with the Government's AI incubator, Google DeepMind and Faculty — is in alpha with a handful of councils, including Dorset, Camden and Barnet, on householder cases. The official line matches this note's: the officer stays the decision-maker, and the tool isn't designed to replace their judgement. That planner-in-control thread is the design principle.

title: The bottom line
paras: So, the bottom line. AI is already a real productivity tool for research and drafting, and ignoring it entirely leaves time on the table. But it's no substitute for professional judgement, and won't be on any horizon this note can honestly see. The planners who benefit understand both the planning and the tool's limits: they use it to reach a first draft faster, and a better-tested argument, while verifying every fact, protecting every confidence, and owning every word. Used that way it makes good planners quicker; used the other way, it makes confident mistakes on your letterhead.

title: Practice points
paras: To pull it together. The tool predicts plausible text, it doesn't verify facts — that's why it hallucinates, so read every output as a draft, not an authority, and verify every case, appeal reference, policy paragraph and figure against the primary source. Never trust a legal or appeal citation from a general model: invented cases are the classic failure, and lawyers have been sanctioned for filing them. Drafting and summarising are the strongest uses, with the facts and judgement supplied by you — but the accountability never leaves you: your name means you own every word, and that engages the professional Code.

Keep personal and confidential data out of public tools, since many retain inputs to train; under data protection law you're the controller, so anonymise or use an enterprise tool whose terms exclude training — and re-check those terms, because they change. Mind the knowledge cut-off, and give the model the source or verify against it. Disclose AI use in appeal evidence, as the Inspectorate now requires. AI rewards the expert and traps the novice, so know the question well enough to spot a wrong answer, guard against skill erosion, and keep a record of your reasoning so the judgement stays yours and defensible. Prefer grounded tools for facts. And it's a tool, not a decision-maker — even the Government's planning AI keeps the officer in charge.

title: Sources
paras: A word on where this rests. It draws on the Planning Inspectorate's guidance on AI in casework evidence — accuracy, disclosure, and the warning that AI can create fake evidence. On the professional body's introduction to planning and AI, its statement that AI must support, not replace, planners, and the Code of Professional Conduct. On the data-protection regulator's guidance and risk toolkit. And on current Government digital work — the Extract tool now live to English authorities, and the decision-support prototype in alpha.

The exact titles, dates and web references all live in the written guide. One caution: capability, tool data-terms and official guidance move quickly — so before relying on this on a live matter, re-check the professional body's and the Inspectorate's current positions, and any tool's data-protection terms.
